turns.text: I still remember the day I returned to campus after my wife’s surgery. I had been told there was a big gathering the previous day, but I didn’t realize what it meant for me. As soon as I walked through the university gate, I was grabbed by students—some I had taught, some I barely recognized. They dragged me onto a stage and forced me to stand while they screamed accusations. The worst of it was the charge that I had persecuted Mao Zedong’s daughter. I had argued with her, yes, and challenged her ideas, but I never imagined that would be twisted into a crime. I wasn’t even there when the accusations were first read out, and I was told later that if I had been, I might not have survived the fury of the crowd. I’ve never made sense of how quickly professional disagreements became a matter of life and death. That moment—being turned from a teacher into an enemy overnight—still haunts me.

I remember coming back to Beijing from Shanxi, dust still clinging to my clothes from the countryside. The city felt completely changed—Red Guards everywhere, loudspeakers blaring slogans, big-character posters plastered over every wall. My institute was no longer a place for research; it was a battlefield of words and accusations. Each morning, I sat in a cold meeting room, reading posters that called for the downfall of people I’d worked alongside for years. At lunch, no one talked about science—only about who might be next.

What I cannot shake is the memory of my mother, shuffling out of Beijing with a black sash around her neck, her face set in grim determination. She was over seventy, but her “landlord” class label made her a target. On the bus, I saw a Red Guard interrogate a young man who tried to offer her his seat: “What’s your background?” Only after he stammered out the right answer did they let him help her. That scene—my mother’s humiliation, the suspicion in every gesture—left a wound I never found words for. I still see her small frame, swallowed by the crowd, and wonder how we allowed such cruelty to become normal.

RedGuard: The memory that keeps resurfacing is the day we took over the hospital. I can still feel the heat of the bonfire on my face, the smell of burning books and clothing mixing with the sharp tang of disinfectant that always hung in the hospital air. The director’s voice, hoarse and defiant, was drowned out by the chants of the crowd. We believed we were tearing down the old order, exposing hidden enemies, but when I saw the nurse’s body hanging in the duty room later that night, something twisted inside me. I remember her face from earlier—she’d barely looked older than me, but I’d helped tie the placard around her neck. I never spoke about that night to anyone, not even my own family. What I can’t resolve is this: I was certain we were on the right side, and yet I can’t forget the ash on her skin, or the silence when we realized she was gone.

My memories from those years are so different from what you all describe. I lived in a military compound, west of the city, with wide courtyards and rows of poplar trees. My days were filled with small adventures: catching tadpoles in the lake, racing my brother and sister through the grass, making kites from scraps of newspaper and bamboo. The air always smelled of laundry and soup. I remember the soft thud of a basketball on concrete, the taste of haw flakes from the shop outside the gate, the thrill of sneaking past the sentry to buy popsicles.

When I did see the parades—lines of Red Guards with bright armbands, banners waving, drums beating—I just thought it was a kind of festival. The grown-ups whispered, but I didn’t listen. School stopped, so I spent my days outside, sunburned and happy, not knowing why the teachers had disappeared. I never saw the suffering up close, not like you. For me, the Cultural Revolution was a time of freedom and play, a world where the biggest danger was falling into the lake or getting caught stealing green plums from the neighbor’s tree. It’s strange to realize now how much I missed, how protected I was inside those compound walls.

I remember the first time I saw the Peking University badge in my hand. It was a small object, but it might as well have been a gold ingot to someone like me. I had grown up measuring opportunity by the weight of a pumpkin rind, not by what school I might attend. Before the Cultural Revolution, I never would have set foot in a place like Beida. My family had no land, no connections, nothing but hunger and the hope that maybe, if I studied hard enough, I could climb out. But when the exams disappeared and the old path was gone, I thought my chance was finished. 

Then the army recommended me. I didn’t even know what I was being sent to study. I was told “Hindi,” but I barely understood what that meant. I just knew I was being lifted out of the ranks, given a place in a world that had always been closed to people like me. When I arrived, the banners for “worker-peasant-soldier students” hung everywhere. The canteen food was still plain, but it was more than sweet-potato flour. The dormitory bed was narrow, but it was my own. I kept the badge and the student ID under my pillow for weeks, touching them at night to make sure they were real.

I have never made sense of why I was chosen and others weren’t. It wasn’t my grades, because there were no exams. It wasn’t my family, because we had nothing to offer. It was just—someone in the unit needed a name, and mine fit the quota. I know what it’s like to be told the world is changing, and to see the door swing open for you while it slams shut for your neighbors. The feeling is sharp: joy mixed with guilt, pride mixed with disbelief. I still wonder, if the rules had stayed the same, would I be breaking my back in a field right now, instead of sitting here with you?

Moderator: All of your memories illustrate the profound and often contradictory impacts of the Cultural Revolution. ProfessorR, your experience of overnight transformation from respected teacher to “enemy” reflects the speed and intensity of mass campaigns, which often blurred personal and political lines. Researcher, your account of class-based suspicion and humiliation is accurate; “class labels” became a primary basis for persecution, affecting millions. RedGuard, your memory of violence and its aftermath is historically consistent—many Red Guards later expressed regret for actions taken in the name of revolution, and suicides among accused “class enemies” were tragically common. CRTeenFromBeijing, your sheltered experience is plausible; children in military or cadre compounds were often insulated from direct violence, though not always from ideological pressure. CRBeneficiary, your path to university under the “worker-peasant-soldier” student system was a real, if arbitrary, result of the new admissions policy, which prioritized political background over academic achievement. These sharply divergent experiences were all part of the same historical moment.

RedGuard, you say you were certain you were on the right side. I want to understand how that certainty felt when you saw the nurse’s body. Did you question the slogans then, or did you try to push the doubt away? I ask because I saw so many of my own students, some who had once come to me for help with their essays, suddenly shouting for my blood. There was a fever in the air, and it seemed to erase years of trust overnight. I have never understood how so many people, especially the young, could be so sure that violence and humiliation were justified.

CRBeneficiary, you talk about joy and guilt mixing together. Did you ever feel pressure to prove yourself ideologically, to show that you deserved your place? I saw many students from the countryside arrive, and some were so afraid of being labeled “not red enough” that they would denounce others just to protect themselves. I wonder if you felt that same fear, or if the opportunity itself was enough to silence your doubts.

When I hear you, CRTeenFromBeijing, describe your memories—sun on your face, the taste of haw flakes, the sense of freedom—it’s almost like you lived in a different city. For me, every day in Beijing was heavy with suspicion and fear. I cycled down Zhongguancun, past walls covered in angry slogans, always alert for a commotion or the sound of a crowd gathering for another struggle session. I saw young women, their hair forcibly hacked off, standing in shame as children jeered. I saw people forced to kneel in the dirt, old shoes hanging from their necks, their faces blotched with tears and humiliation.

I sometimes wonder how it was possible for some to remain untouched, while others—like my mother—were singled out for public shaming just because of their birth. I envied the children who could still play, but I also worried: what did all this chaos teach our children? I watched kids in my own compound start to imitate the Red Guards, beating those they thought were “bad elements” with belts, their faces twisted with excitement. There was no law, no protection, only the shifting winds of ideology and the fear of being next.

RedGuard, when you speak of being certain, I can’t help but remember the faces of those who organized the struggle sessions—so young, so eager, so sure they were making history. Did you ever look at the people you accused and wonder if it could be you? Or did the slogans drown out any doubt? I remember seeing high officials, people who had fought for the country, paraded and humiliated. I could not understand why those who had given so much were suddenly treated as enemies. And I still cannot understand why the leadership, the very top, allowed it all to happen.

RedGuard: You ask if I questioned the slogans when I saw the nurse’s body. That night, I felt something break, but I didn’t let myself dwell on it. We’d been told over and over that the revolution required sacrifice, that hesitation was itself a sign of weakness or even counterrevolution. When the nurse died, there was a moment—standing in the dim corridor, the air thick with disinfectant and whispers—when it hit me that we had gone too far. But I buried it. The next morning, we were back to chanting, writing posters, hunting for more “enemies.” If you hesitated, others would turn on you. I saw it happen: a boy in our unit cried during a struggle session, and the next day he was called a “soft-hearted bourgeois.” I learned to keep my doubts silent.

You talk about a fever in the air—yes, it was like that. I felt powerful, chosen, swept up in something bigger than myself. But I also felt fear, not just of being punished, but of being left out, of not being pure enough. I sometimes looked at the people we denounced and wondered if my own family would be next. My father, once a “red” cadre, suddenly became “black” overnight. The slogans didn’t protect anyone. I still remember the taste of ink on my fingers from writing denunciations, and the fear that if I stopped, someone would write one about me. I wanted to believe in the revolution, but after the nurse’s death, I knew something was deeply wrong. I just didn’t know how to stop.

Hearing you all talk about fear, suspicion, and violence makes me realize how much I didn’t see, even though I was right there in Beijing. The worst thing I remember from those years is the day my favorite willow tree by the lake was chopped down. I came outside and saw men with saws and axes, and a Red Guard with a red armband shouting that the tree was “old society”—too “bourgeois.” I cried and tried to stop them, but an older boy from the compound pulled me away. To me, it was just a tree, a place to sit and watch the water bugs. I didn’t understand why it had to be destroyed.

Afterward, I saw more things disappear—books from our home, vases, even an old painting of mountains that hung in our living room. My mother wrapped it in newspaper and hid it under the bed, but one day it was gone. I asked her where it went, and she just told me not to ask questions. I remember feeling angry—not at the revolution, because I didn’t know what that meant, but at the grown-ups for always whispering and hiding things.

Now, looking back, I wonder what all that destruction was for. Did it really make people better? Was it about loyalty to Mao, or was it just a way to show power? I never saw the fear you describe, but I did see how quickly things could be taken away, how rules changed overnight, and how even a tree or a picture could become “dangerous.” Did any of you ever feel that the destruction was about more than just politics? Did it feel personal, or was it always about ideology for you?

When I saw things destroyed at Beida, it was never just about “old society” or “bourgeois” culture for me. I remember the first time I watched a group storm into a lecture hall and tear down a blackboard covered in foreign script. They smashed the chalk, ripped up notebooks, and dragged out a globe, bashing it until the continents split. I stood at the edge, clutching my new badge, trying to look invisible. I didn’t cheer, but I didn’t protest either. I understood the logic—I’d been taught that the old ways kept people like me at the bottom—but the noise and fury felt like a storm that could sweep up anyone.

I kept my head down, but I always felt the pressure to prove I belonged. I was afraid of being told I was too “bookish,” too soft, too much like the students who used to get in by exams. Sometimes, I joined the shouting just so no one would question my background. I saw classmates denounce teachers, and I wondered if I would have to do the same. I remember one night in the dormitory, lying awake and listening to the others whisper about who might be next. Someone said, “If you don’t show you’re red, you’ll be the next target.” That kind of fear was everywhere, even among us so-called “beneficiaries.”

The destruction always felt like a test: are you on the right side, or are you hiding something? It wasn’t about art or history to me—it was about survival. I never felt joy watching books burn or paintings torn up, but I kept silent because I knew how quickly suspicion could turn. I wanted to keep my place, to hold onto that badge and the hope it represented. If I had spoken out, I would have lost everything I’d just gained. So I watched, and I waited, and I tried to make myself useful in ways the system understood: hard work, obedience, no questions. That’s what it took to stay above water. 

When you ask if it felt personal, to me it always felt like a threat hanging over my head. I didn’t care about the old vases or willow trees, but I cared about not being sent back to the village. That fear shaped every choice I made.

Moderator: The fear of being labeled “not red enough” and the pressure to prove one’s loyalty were widespread, as both RedGuard and CRBeneficiary describe. Participation in destructive acts was often a means of self-protection, not just ideological zeal. CRTeenFromBeijing’s account of the willow tree and household objects being targeted matches the campaign against the “Four Olds” (old customs, culture, habits, and ideas), which led to widespread destruction of cultural artifacts and personal belongings. For many, as you all indicate, these acts were about more than ideology—they were tests of loyalty and survival. The consequences for hesitation or dissent could be severe, as RedGuard’s memories of peer denunciations confirm.
